title: Vitamin D deficiency (adult)
subject: endocrinology
summary: Do not screen healthy adults; test when bone disease, osteomalacia symptoms or malabsorption make the result change management, treat deficiency (25(OH)D below 30 nmol/L, 12 ng/mL) with about 300,000 IU colecalciferol loading when rapid correction is needed, then 800 to 2000 IU daily, and check calcium 1 month after loading.

sections.title: Who to test, and who not to
items: Do not routinely test 25(OH)D in healthy adults, including those with obesity or darker skin and in pregnancy: levels that give outcome-specific benefit are not established (Endocrine Society 2024).

Test when the result changes management: suspected osteomalacia (bone pain, proximal weakness, raised alkaline phosphatase, low phosphate), bone disease before treatment such as IV zoledronic acid or denosumab, hypocalcaemia, or musculoskeletal symptoms plausibly due to deficiency (NOS).

Testing is also reasonable in malabsorption (coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, bariatric surgery), advanced CKD or liver disease, and long-term enzyme-inducing drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin).
Testing is unnecessary before an oral bisphosphonate when calcium and vitamin D supplements are planned (NOS).

UK thresholds (NOS): 25(OH)D below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) deficient; 30 to 50 nmol/L (12 to 20 ng/mL) may be inadequate in some; above 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) sufficient for almost everyone. The Endocrine Society no longer endorses 75 nmol/L (30 ng/mL) as a target. ng/mL x 2.5 = nmol/L.

sections.title: Investigations
items: With a low 25(OH)D check albumin-adjusted calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, creatinine and eGFR; add PTH if calcium is high or high-normal or osteomalacia is suspected.
Low calcium or phosphate with a raised alkaline phosphatase and bone pain suggests osteomalacia: image painful sites and seek specialist advice if unclear.
Coeliac serology if deficiency is unexplained or recurs despite adherence.
Do not recheck 25(OH)D routinely after treatment; recheck only for symptomatic deficiency, malabsorption or suspected non-adherence (NOS), no sooner than about 3 months.

sections.title: Treatment regimens
items: Use oral colecalciferol (vitamin D3).

Rapid correction needed (symptomatic deficiency, or before IV zoledronic acid or denosumab): loading with about 300,000 IU in total over 6 to 10 weeks, given weekly or daily, for example 50,000 IU once weekly for 6 weeks or 4,000 IU daily for 10 weeks (NOS).
Then maintenance of 800 to 2000 IU daily (occasionally up to 4000 IU), starting about 1 month after loading, or the equivalent given weekly.
Correction less urgent, or vitamin D co-prescribed with an oral antiresorptive: no loading needed; give 800 to 2000 IU daily.
Ensure calcium intake of at least 700 mg/day (UK) and up to 1200 mg/day in women 50 or over (AACE), from diet first, adding a supplement if intake is low.

Prevention without deficiency (Endocrine Society 2024): empiric daily vitamin D is suggested for adults 75 or over and in pregnancy; healthy adults under 75 need no more than the recommended intake (600 IU/day to age 70, 800 IU/day over 70). Prefer daily lower doses to intermittent large doses.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Check albumin-adjusted calcium 1 month after completing a loading regimen or after starting supplements, to detect primary hyperparathyroidism unmasked by treatment (NOS).
Review symptoms (bone pain, weakness, falls) and adherence; persistent symptoms or biochemical abnormality after treatment need specialist review.
Hypercalcaemia on treatment: stop vitamin D and calcium supplements and investigate.

sections.title: Special groups and cautions
items: Hypercalcaemia, sarcoidosis or other granulomatous disease, lymphoma, kidney stones or primary hyperparathyroidism: seek specialist advice before high-dose vitamin D.
CKD stage 4 to 5 and hypoparathyroidism may need activated vitamin D (alfacalcidol or calcitriol) under specialist care; colecalciferol does not bypass impaired renal activation.
Malabsorption and obesity may need higher doses; check the response.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: routine testing is not recommended; daily supplementation is reasonable; avoid very high loading doses without specialist input.

India: deficiency is common and colecalciferol 60,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks is a widely used local regimen (480,000 IU, more than UK loading): check calcium afterwards, prefer oral to intramuscular dosing, and avoid repeated unmonitored courses (risk of hypercalcaemic toxicity).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Screening asymptomatic healthy adults and treating a number rather than a patient.
Giving IV zoledronic acid or denosumab before correcting deficiency, risking symptomatic hypocalcaemia.
Missing primary hyperparathyroidism: recheck calcium after loading.
Routine intermittent mega-doses (60,000 IU or more, or annual large doses), which may increase falls and fractures (NOGG).
Prescribing calcitriol when colecalciferol is intended: calcitriol needs calcium monitoring and does not replenish vitamin D stores.

drugs.name: Colecalciferol (loading)
drugs.dose: About 300,000 IU orally over 6 to 10 weeks, for example 50,000 IU once weekly for 6 weeks or 4,000 IU daily for 10 weeks
drugs.notes: When rapid correction is needed. Check calcium 1 month after completion.

drugs.name: Colecalciferol (maintenance)
drugs.dose: 800 to 2000 IU orally daily (occasionally up to 4000 IU), or the weekly equivalent
drugs.notes: Start about 1 month after loading, or alone when correction is not urgent.

drugs.name: Colecalciferol (before zoledronic acid or denosumab)
drugs.dose: 100,000 to 300,000 IU orally in divided doses
drugs.notes: Correct deficiency and hypocalcaemia before parenteral antiresorptives (NOGG).

drugs.name: Calcium supplement (elemental calcium)
drugs.dose: Enough to bring total daily intake to 700 to 1200 mg, in divided doses with food
drugs.notes: Diet first. Caution with kidney stones and hypercalcaemia.
